nameStory: Prairie woundwort gets its name from two sources: its original home on Midwestern prairies and the old belief that it could heal wounds. The 'wort' part is an Old English word meaning 'plant' or 'herb,' which you'll find in many plant names like St. John's wort and mugwort.
description: Prairie woundwort is a sturdy perennial herb that stands 1-3 feet tall with a square stem typical of the mint family. It produces spikes of small pink to purple flowers arranged in clusters around the stem, blooming from summer into early fall. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance but displays attractive tubular flowers that buzz with pollinator activity. Like other mints, it can spread by underground runners to form small colonies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple tubular flowers cluster in dense whorls around the square stem, creating interrupted spikes. Each flower has a hooded upper lip and a spotted lower lip that serves as a landing pad for bees.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves grow opposite each other on the square stem. They feel soft and somewhat fuzzy due to fine hairs, with toothed edges that give them a serrated appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: The distinctive square stem feels rigid between your fingers and has a slight minty scent when crushed, though not as strong as other mint family members.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small nutlets develop where the flowers were, arranged in groups of four within the old flower clusters that persist into fall.

habitat: Prairie woundwort favors disturbed soils and edges in New England, appearing along roadsides, field margins, and waste places. It's quite rare here, preferring drier, well-drained soils compared to its wetland-loving cousin marsh woundwort. You're most likely to spot it in areas with some disturbance, as it's somewhat weedy in nature.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge with distinctively square stems and fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs. Plants begin building height through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Flowering begins in mid-summer with pink-purple flower spikes that continue developing through the season. This is the best time for identification when flowers are fresh and vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but seed clusters remain visible on the stems. Leaves may yellow but the square stems and seed arrangement are still diagnostic features.
seasonality.winter: Stems die back to the ground, leaving only underground parts alive. Look for dried flower spike remnants that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Despite being called 'prairie' woundwort, this plant is so rare in New England that it's been documented only 7 times across the entire region - making it one of our most elusive wildflowers!
confusionNotes: Prairie woundwort is most easily confused with marsh woundwort, but prairie prefers drier sites while marsh loves wet feet. Prairie woundwort also has softer, more heart-shaped leaves compared to marsh woundwort's narrower, lance-shaped leaves.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of prairie woundwort in New England reflects our region's distance from its natural Midwestern prairie home. Most populations here are likely introductions that struggle to establish in our different climate and soil conditions.
compareHints: Prairie woundwort differs from marsh woundwort by preferring dry rather than wet habitats and having broader, more heart-shaped leaves. Unlike hyssop-leaved hedge-nettle, prairie woundwort has distinctly toothed leaf margins rather than smooth edges. Its fuzzy texture also sets it apart from the smoother-leaved marsh species in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hedge-nettle relatives, this species stands out for its narrow, hyssop-like leaves and preference for wetter habitats.
Marsh woundwort differs from its hedge-nettle cousins by its preference for consistently wet habitats rather than just moist woodland edges.
Unlike other hedgenettles in New England, woolly hedgenettle is the only one with thick, densely woolly leaves that feel soft to touch.
Among New England's hedge nettles, marsh hedge nettle stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, soft-textured leaves and stems compared to its smoother relatives.
